text: LTV Industries, running one production instance, has just acquired a subsidiary in a country with a strict data-residency law: certain personal data must physically stay within that country's borders. The subsidiary runs its own HR and incident process, reuses some of the parent's ITSM concepts, and will eventually need limited reporting shared back to parent leadership. You're the architect recommending the platform strategy.

Step one: is a second production instance justified? Domain Separation only partitions data logically within one instance's existing region — it doesn't relocate underlying storage. If the parent's instance region can't satisfy the subsidiary's residency requirement, no amount of logical separation fixes that. This is the rare case where a second, regional production instance is the right call, because the law leaves no other path.

Step two: contrast this with a far more typical acquisition. Without a residency constraint, the default from earlier in this chapter applies cleanly — don't stand up a second production instance just because it's a different legal entity. Domain Separation inside the existing instance would almost certainly suffice instead. The residency law is the one fact that flips this scenario's answer.

Step three: even with a second instance, the scope-boundary question still applies inside it. The subsidiary's HR and incident apps are owned by its own team on its own release cadence, so they get their own scoped applications. Shared ITSM logic the parent already built well gets published as its own versioned scoped application, and the subsidiary pulls a specific, pinned version rather than rebuilding it or depending on an always-changing copy.

Notice the order: the residency law decides instance strategy first, because it can't be solved logically. Domain Separation is evaluated next, within each instance individually. Scope boundaries come last, based on real team ownership, regardless of which instance those scoped applications end up living on. Getting that order backward means solving the wrong layer of the problem first.
That closes Platform Architecture. Next, Chapter 3 begins with Data Architecture, starting at Table Design for Scale.
